newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka MPs trade charges after killing.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka MPs trade charges after killing.

text.p: Lawmakers of Sri Lanka's ruling People's Alliance blamed the main opposition party for this week's political killing and riots, saying it failed to defuse a "culture of violence" during 17 years in power.
People's Alliance lawmakers accused the United National Party (UNP) of failing to contain the "culture of violence and assassinations" before being ousted by the alliance in 1994 elections.
"The democratic values in this country have been slowly dying ever since the UNP came to power in 1977," Jagath Balasuriya, an MP from the People's Alliance, told Reuters.

The killing of People's Alliance lawmaker Nalanda Ellawala sparked riots in the gem mining town of Ratnapura, 80 km (50 miles) southeast of Colombo, this week with angry ruling party supporters burning buildings belonging to rival UNP supporters.
Gunmen shot and killed Ellawala, 29, on Tuesday during a roadside quarrel near Ratnapura between his supporters and rivals from the UNP.

Police have named two suspects, UNP lawmaker Susantha Punchinilame and the UNP's mayoral candidate for Ratnapura, Mahinda Ratnatilleke, and offered a one million rupee ($17,500) reward for information leading to their arrest.
Police arrested seven junior UNP activists on Friday in connection with the lawmaker's murder, but the two named suspects were not among them.
UNP members lashed back at the alliance, saying it was blowing Tuesday's killing out of proportion to win sympathy ahead of local elections in March.

The killing came the day before a deadline for filing nominations in the March 21 local elections, the first electoral contest between the UNP and the alliance since 1994 when the alliance ousted the UNP.
On Friday, the UNP suspended the party memberships of the two suspects, a day after party leader and former prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe called on the two to turn themselves in.
"Now we would like to leave the matter up to police and courts and carry on with a peaceful election," senior UNP MP Karunasena Kodituwakku said in an interview.
"Unfortunately, the government is....blowing it out of proportion to cover up their own weaknesses and unpopularity."
But PA lawmakers insisted they were not going to forget the killing of Ellawala.
"This incident happened in broad daylight and this is an unprecedented act of political violence," Balasuriya said.
Analysts see this week's violence as an extension of the bitterness the two parties have always felt towards each other.

"Sri Lankan politics have long become akin to a Cold War between two main political parties and frequently punctuated by hot wars. Ratnapura is only the latest tragic case in point," said political analyst Dayan Jayatilake.
"The bitter acrimony that exists between the PA and the UNP should end," the independent Island newspaper said in an editorial on Friday.
